sections.body_md:
A symmetric matrix defines a quadratic form \(x^T A x\). The form is positive definite when that number is positive for every nonzero \(x\), and positive semidefinite when it is only nonnegative. Indefinite means the form takes both signs.

The eigenvalue test is the practical version. In an orthonormal eigenbasis the form becomes a sum of \(\lambda_i y_i^2\). Every term is nonnegative for every \(y\) exactly when every eigenvalue is nonnegative, and every term is positive for \(y \ne 0\) exactly when every eigenvalue is positive. A single negative eigenvalue produces a direction in which the form is negative.

When every eigenvalue is positive, a positive level set of the form is an ellipsoid. Its axes lie along the eigenvectors, and a large eigenvalue makes the ellipsoid short in that direction, because the same budget \(c\) is spent faster.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\(A\) is positive definite when \(x^T A x > 0\) for all \(x \ne 0\), and positive semidefinite when \(x^T A x \ge 0\) for all \(x\). Equivalently, every eigenvalue is positive, or every eigenvalue is nonnegative. For the diagonal case \(A = \mathrm{diag}(\alpha, \beta)\) with \(\alpha, \beta > 0\),
\[
\alpha x_1^2 + \beta x_2^2 = c
\]
is an ellipse with semi-axes \(\sqrt{c/\alpha}\) and \(\sqrt{c/\beta}\). A negative determinant of a \(2 \times 2\) symmetric matrix means the eigenvalues have opposite signs.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Let \(A = \mathrm{diag}(3, 12)\). Both diagonal entries are positive, so both eigenvalues are positive and \(A\) is positive definite. At \((1,1)\) the quadratic form equals 15.

The level set \(3 x_1^2 + 12 x_2^2 = 27\) divides through by 27 to give \(x_1^2/9 + x_2^2/2.25 = 1\). The semi-axis along \(x_1\) has length 3. The semi-axis along \(x_2\) has length 1.5, the square root of \(2.25\). The shorter axis is the one with the larger eigenvalue, 12 rather than 3.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: A positive determinant is not enough: a \(2 \times 2\) negative definite matrix also has positive determinant, and its trace is negative. Positive entries do not imply positive eigenvalues. A zero eigenvalue is the boundary between definite and semidefinite; the form vanishes on that eigenvector. The ellipse axes follow the eigenvectors, which need not be the coordinate axes when \(A\) has off-diagonal entries. Leading principal minors are an alternative test, and skipping one of them can accept an indefinite matrix.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: A twice differentiable function is convex on an open convex set when its Hessian is positive semidefinite everywhere. A positive definite matrix also supplies descent directions: if \(D\) is positive definite and \(g \ne 0\), then \(g^T(-Dg) < 0\). The same hypothesis makes \(u^T A v\) an inner product, which is the pairing used to talk about conjugacy of search directions.
